content_voiceover: This question tests familiarity with the third edition World Federation of Hemophilia guidelines for pediatric patients. Several statements are presented and the fellow must identify which combination is correct. Comprehensive multidisciplinary checkups, covering hematologic, musculoskeletal, and quality of life assessments, should occur at least every six months in children, and this is correct. Early initiation of prophylaxis with clotting factor concentrates, ideally before age three and before the onset of joint disease, is a core WFH recommendation to prevent spontaneous and breakthrough bleeding including hemarthrosis. Both of these statements are accurate. The statement about suspected central nervous system bleeding is the trap in this question. The guideline actually recommends giving clotting factor replacement immediately, before imaging like a brain CT, precisely because CNS bleeding can be rapidly life threatening and treatment should never be delayed to obtain imaging first. Finally, children with hemophilia should receive the same routine vaccination schedule as the general population, but preferably by the subcutaneous route rather than intramuscular or intradermal injection, since this is equally safe and effective and avoids the need for prophylactic clotting factor coverage.
keypoints: Multidisciplinary review at least every 6 months in pediatric hemophilia
Start prophylaxis early, ideally before age 3 and before joint disease
Suspected CNS bleed: treat first with factor replacement, then image
Routine vaccines are fine but preferably given subcutaneously
keypoint_voiceover: For pediatric hemophilia care per WFH guidelines, remember to schedule multidisciplinary checkups every six months, start prophylaxis early to prevent joint disease, and never delay factor replacement for imaging when CNS bleeding is suspected, treat first, then scan. Vaccines should be given on schedule, just favor the subcutaneous route over intramuscular.
